thermal-contact: Could a whole cool block store more energy than a tiny hot bead? Look at which way energy first moves when they touch.
Picture a bead dropped into a huge tank of water. Which body's temperature would change more?
kelvin-differences: Try moving both thermometer readings to a scale whose zero means absolute zero.
A ratio compares two readings by division. Which two absolute readings would you divide?
heat-internal-energy: Trace the energy from the hand turning the stirrer into the liquid.
Imagine how your arm feels after stirring thick syrup. Where did the energy for that effort go?
state-equilibrium: A gas can absorb heat on the way out and release heat on the way back. Which quantity depends only on its final state?
Picture a piston moving out and back under different pressures. What does returning to the same state guarantee?
pressure-area: Pressure tells you the push on each square centimeter. Sketch how many squares receive that push.
Compare the push on one square centimeter with the total push on the whole piston.
moles-particles: Imagine two bags with equal numbers of marbles, with heavier marbles in one bag. Would a scale give equal readings?
Try squeezing one of the samples. Which measurement still counts the molecules inside?
ideal-gas-law: At fixed volume, picture warmer particles hitting the same wall harder. Which way would the pressure change?
A sealed container keeps its particles. What changes about their impacts when the gas warms?
ideal-gas-limits: Compare the measurement with the assumptions in the gas model. Which could you check experimentally?
Look at the temperature that went into the formula. When does the formula require an absolute reading?
random-motion: Follow just one particle for a second. How far does it travel in that time?
Add the distances traveled in one second. Can motion to the left cancel any of that distance?
wall-momentum: Count all the pushes on the wall in one second. What changes when the gap between hits is shorter?
Compare the total impulse in a second with one hit and with two identical hits.
kinetic-temperature: Compare a heavy and a light particle with the same kinetic energy. How would mass affect their speeds?
Picture a single gas at one temperature. Could its particles collide at a range of speeds?
speed-averages: Start by squaring the speed of each particle. Does a change of direction change that square?
Nine is a squared speed. What does the final word in “root mean square” ask you to do?
internal-versus-bulk: Imagine riding inside the accelerating box. Did the random motion that a thermometer senses change?
Separate the motion of the whole box from motion measured by someone inside it.
expansion-work: Draw the gas force on the piston and the direction the piston moves during compression.
A weight pushes the piston inward through a distance. What does that tell you about energy transfer?
external-reversible: Run the rubbing piston backward in your mind. What happens to the energy that warmed its sides?
A thermometer records the rubbing. Could recording the temperature undo the rubbing?
heat-capacity: Picture warming two identical cups separately. Add the heat needed for each cup.
Try treating the extra mass as a second identical sample. What would warm it?
first-law: Draw an arrow showing where the 60 joules go. Is the system giving them away or receiving them?
Insulation blocks heat transfer. Trace the other transfer named in the question.
path-state: Write the balance as energy gained equals heat in minus work delivered. Hold the left side fixed.
Use the same heat input on both paths and subtract their different amounts of work. Would the gains match?
constant-volume: A rigid wall keeps the volume fixed. Follow the heater wires across that wall.
Ask what drives energy through a wire connected to a power supply.
constant-pressure: Trace the heat entering the gas. One portion stays inside and another pushes the piston. How do those portions combine?
The 50 joules count only energy stored. Where did the energy to move the piston come from?
cp-cv-assumptions: Compare a single atom with a molecule that can also rotate or vibrate. How might each store energy?
Changing a thermometer scale leaves a molecule's possible motions unchanged. Which motions can absorb energy?
isothermal-work: Draw the gas pushing outward while the piston moves inward. Then use the fixed temperature to balance energy.
Fixed temperature keeps an ideal gas's internal energy steady. Can two energy transfers balance each other?
adiabatic-change: Ask what could take energy away when the wall is insulated and the space ahead is empty.
Picture a gas rushing into empty space. Could you reverse each tiny step by nudging the pressure?
steady-conduction: Spread the same temperature drop across a longer distance. Does the temperature change more or less per centimeter?
Compare a thin and a thick layer of the same insulation between the same temperatures.
thermal-resistance: Imagine adding a second layer of insulation to the first. Which way should heat flow change?
The end temperatures are fixed. Is the total resistance between them also fixed?
empirical-convection: Think about a breeze over warm skin. What changed in the air against the surface?
Compare still air with fast-moving air at the same temperature. Would they carry heat away equally well?
radiative-balance: Find the radiation coming back from the surroundings. Which body's temperature sets that part?
Check how the radiation emitted by the object depends on its absolute temperature.
lumped-gray-limits: A thermometer at the center and one at the edge give different readings. Which would represent the whole sample?
Can a final thermometer reading tell you how hot the center and surface each were earlier?
reversible-comparison: Imagine heat rushing between objects at very different temperatures. Could you reverse that transfer with a tiny change?
Two paths can have the same endpoints. Which kind of path does the heat-over-temperature calculation assume?
entropy-heat: Write the entropy change as heat divided by absolute temperature. Which number is now larger in the denominator?
Compare 600 divided by each temperature. Does knowing the heat alone give the result?
entropy-production: An isolated system must pass two checks. After balancing energy, check the allowed direction of entropy change.
Compare the units of entropy and energy. Which quantity does the proposed change describe?
system-surroundings: Compare the entropy one reservoir loses with what the other gains as their temperatures become nearly equal.
Write a heat-over-temperature term for each reservoir. What else besides heat appears?
engine-energy: Draw the energy in and work out as arrows. How could the longer outgoing arrow be supplied?
After a full cycle, how much extra stored energy does the engine have available to spend?
carnot-bound: Work out the largest possible fraction from the two reservoir temperatures before judging the claim.
Which scale measures both temperatures from absolute zero for the efficiency ratio?
refrigerator-cop: Trace heat from the food to the room. Which energy transfer does the refrigerator's performance number count?
Write the units for heat moved and for work supplied. What happens to those units when you divide?
energy-usefulness: Imagine warm water cooling all the way to room temperature. What change in the setup limits the engine?
Compare one joule in a warm cup with one joule in a hot cup. What physical difference matters to the engine?
micro-macro: Reading the labels on switches gives information. Would reading them change their positions?
Count the physical switches before and after learning their labels. What became more precise?
count-arrangements: Label the switches A through D. Can choosing A as the one up be distinguished from choosing B?
List only arrangements with one switch up. Which choices would count the same arrangement twice?
boltzmann-entropy: Start with the entropy for each count. How do you subtract one logarithm from another?
Which operation on the two counts corresponds to subtracting their logarithms?
fluctuations: A fourfold change applies directly to the variance. What extra operation takes you to standard deviation?
Imagine repeating a coin experiment with many more flips. Would the spread in the total count stay fixed?
reservoir-model: Picture the small system exchanging energy with its surroundings while its average stays steady.
List the possible energy readings first. What would make one particular outcome appear more often?
positive-temperature-domain: Look at the denominator when the absolute temperature reaches zero. Is that division defined?
What temperature scale does the formula require, and what would changing the unit do to its physical meaning?
boltzmann-weights: Compare the weight of one state with the total weight. Where does the common multiplier appear?
Add the normalized weights after shifting the reference. What does the denominator count?
partition-function: Give the two upper states separate labels. Which outcomes would count as finding the upper energy?
Imagine tallying upper-energy readings when there are multiple ways to get that reading.
mean-energy-capacity: Make a list of repeated readings. What happens to the average when the excited reading appears more often?
List the two possible readings before and after changing their chances. Which part of the list changed?
phase-latent-heat: Imagine marking the melted and solid portions in two colors. Which portion used energy to change form?
Watch ice as it melts. What can added energy change while the thermometer stays steady?
free-energy: Write the two terms in the free energy. Could a state with more possible arrangements have an advantage?
Changing the scale on a thermometer leaves the sample unchanged. What other property enters the free energy?
chemical-potential: Imagine two regions of very different sizes. Must matching their particle counts stop exchange?
Imagine moving one particle across the boundary. Which change would tell you whether the move is favored?
mean-occupation: Consider several distinct states together. Which restriction applies to this one specified state?
List the possible whole-number counts for this state. Where can their weighted average fall?
quantum-distribution-domains: List possible particle counts in one state. Could their average fall below all of them?
Check which particles the given formula describes. What input caused its output to become unphysical?
classical-quantum-map: Compare the size of 1 with 1.1. Would dropping 1 make only a tiny change?
Try both adding 1 to 1.1 and subtracting 1. Are those close enough to treat alike?
third-law: Imagine halving a distance again and again. Does a statement about the limit tell you the last finite step?
The stated result counts possible lowest-energy states. What does that tell you about the steps a refrigerator can take?
choose-boundary: Draw the system boundary around the kettle and follow a bit of steam through it.
Would a scale notice the escaping steam? What else travels with that mass?
combine-thermal: Track what passes through the leak. Does it change how a thermometer is calibrated?
Try balancing energy while counting the gas that leaves. What assumption about the contents needs updating?
cycle-audit: Check the energy subtraction, then calculate the best possible efficiency at the two stated temperatures.
Compute the fraction that becomes work and compare it with the limit set by the reservoirs.
thermal-assessment: Try a slightly larger heat capacity with the same heater reading. Would the predicted temperature rise shift?
Keep the digits on the display and vary the heat capacity within its uncertainty. What changes?
